name: Alpha-ketoglutarate
lead: Alpha-ketoglutarate (AKG, also 2-oxoglutarate) is an organic acid that occurs naturally in the body as an intermediate of the citric acid cycle and as a hub linking energy metabolism with amino acid and nitrogen handling.[1] It is also sold as an over-the-counter supplement, usually as a calcium salt, and has attracted interest in longevity circles.[2][3]

Interest rose after a 2020 study reported that dietary calcium AKG extended lifespan and reduced frailty in ageing mice.[14] Reviews of AKG as a human supplement note that the human literature is thin, consisting of a few older studies on muscle, wound healing and post-surgical recovery, with no recent published trials demonstrating effects on ageing or age-related disease.[5]

No study has tested AKG for cosmetic or appearance outcomes. Wikipedia's article states there are currently no randomized controlled trials showing pharmacological effects of AKG in humans.[1] Several trials in older or middle-aged adults are registered or ongoing.[11]

paras: AKG is marketed as a longevity supplement, with claims relating to healthspan, muscle and recovery. Older human studies from the 1980s and 1990s examined it for muscle growth, wound healing and recovery after surgery, according to a review.[5] Salts such as arginine AKG and ornithine AKG appear in sports and pre-workout supplements.[7] One US-labelled over-the-counter growth-hormone-support product lists ornithine alpha-ketoglutarate among its ingredients.[18]

AKG is produced from isocitrate in the citric acid cycle and from glutamate by transamination and glutaminolysis, and it feeds amino acid synthesis and ammonia handling.[1] It can act as a non-enzymatic antioxidant by reacting with hydrogen peroxide, and it is a precursor of the neurotransmitter GABA.[1]

AKG is a required cofactor for the 2-oxoglutarate-dependent oxygenases, a large enzyme family that includes collagen hydroxylases, histone demethylases and TET DNA-demethylating enzymes, linking it to epigenetic regulation.[4][1] It also activates the receptor OXGR1.[1] Mutations in IDH enzymes in some cancers produce 2-hydroxyglutarate, an AKG competitor, which has been a focus of cancer biology.[16][17]
Short-term tolerability is described as generally good in the limited literature, but long-term human safety data are lacking.[5] No adverse-effect trials in cosmetic users have been published.

A review concluded that there are no recently published studies demonstrating a role for AKG in treating ageing or age-related diseases in humans and called for clinical studies.[5] The key lifespan finding comes from mice, in which calcium AKG extended lifespan and compressed morbidity.[14]

Registered human trials include a placebo-controlled phase 2 trial of AKG in middle-aged adults examining biological age (n=120),[10] a recruitment evaluation paper for a randomized gerotherapeutic trial in biologically older adults (the ABLE trial),[11] a small completed study of calcium AKG and ageing markers (n=34),[12] and trials in cardiac surgery, aortic aneurysm, hypertension and eye disease.[13][15] Results of most were not available in the sources reviewed.
Sports-nutrition trials have used arginine AKG as one of several ingredients in a pre-workout blend, which cannot isolate AKG's effect.[7] Appearance outcomes have not been studied.

timeline.event: Cell Metabolism study reports calcium AKG extends lifespan and compresses morbidity in mice.[14]
Review concludes human evidence of AKG for ageing is lacking.[5]
